fatal_errors: The proposed approximately 700 °C chloride-containing sulfuric-acid electrolyte is incompatible with the immersed aqueous tribocorrosion experiment and is not physically defined without extraordinary pressure and chemical-stability controls.

The target comparison was AlCoCrFeNi2.1 versus identically conditioned DS2205 in deionized water at 25–100 °C, whereas the hypothesis substitutes a homogenized HEA and an aggressive acid/chloride environment.
The proposed dominant micro-galvanic selective-dissolution mechanism conflicts with the observed robust passivation and low degradation of the retained L12/B2 lamellar HEA.

The cited evidence concerns static corrosion and selective dissolution at much lower temperatures; it does not establish wear-induced galvanic acceleration under the proposed 700 °C tribocorrosion conditions.
explanation: The response addresses coupled wear and corrosion and gives a testable film-removal/micro-galvanic feedback hypothesis, but it does not reconstruct the study. The actual temperature dependence arose from competition among depassivation, repassivation, and tribo-layer stability: abrasion at 25 °C, minimum-wear polishing near 50 °C, and repeated oxide/tribo-layer fracture at 100 °C. The HEA retained its lamellar phase structure and outperformed DS2205 by roughly an order of magnitude in wear rate, rather than being shown to degrade through dominant interphase galvanic attack. The homogenized-control experiment has some discriminating value, but homogenization would also change phase constitution, hardness, passivation chemistry, and wear resistance, so it cannot isolate galvanic coupling without additional controls such as wear-only, corrosion-only, phase-potential mapping, and matched mechanical properties. E1 and E2 support possible Al–Ni-rich selective dissolution in related alloys, but neither validates the proposed tribocorrosion feedback or the stated 700 °C boundary.
